events.credibility_reason: Specific identified errors in the key step, unanswered: Innami et al. (2010) give evidence against the continuity of minimum inner spanning tree length that the proof relies on; de Wet's thesis gives counterexamples to the inner-spanning-tree claim; Ivanov-Tuzhilin trace contradictory requirements on the 'characteristic area'. No published defence found; the 2025 survey and 2026 paper call the conjecture open.
Known only through Ivanov-Tuzhilin, who say it repeats the Du-Hwang mistake and checks monotonicity only on a 5-gon; its own claims were not read.

The repository README says verification is done only at the boundary f = d 'rather than checking the entire box'; extracts say 4-point lemmas are proven only at f = d, that some high-complexity cases are excluded, and that symbolic verification was not done for variable f. The 'entire parameter space' claim could not be re-located. The only human checks are the authors' own. Serious method from established researchers with no identified error, so it is kept.
events.ai_basis: We conducted experiments using GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Pro. (Abstract/ICML: LLMs generate rule-constrained geometric lemmas implemented as executable code, which become the verification functions yielding the certified bound; authors manually check every LLM-proposed lemma.)

why: The statement asks for the exact value sqrt(3)/2, so lower bounds (0.8, 0.824/0.842, 0.8559) are bounds and the 5-, 6- and <=7-point proofs are cases. The 1990/92 Du-Hwang claim would be whole, but it is knocked down: several independent published critiques identify specific failures in its key lemma (including counterexamples to the inner-spanning-tree claim), and no defence has appeared. The critiques and the 2025 survey settle nothing, so they are none. The 2026 Ke et al. event is a bound. ICML poster acceptance at an ML venue is not a reading of the geometry, so it is unreviewed. It is doubtful rather than not credible, because the repository and the paper themselves admit that verification was restricted to the boundary f = d. The AI call was close between generated and assisted. By the authors' account the LLMs produced the lemmas that make up the certificate and humans checked them, inside a pipeline the humans designed. I chose generated because the lemmas are the mathematical content of the bound. Assisted would be defensible, and the quote names the models without saying which lemma each one produced.
doubts: Whether the 0.8559 certificate covers all configurations or only the boundary f = d is unresolved. If it does not, it is arguably closer to a restricted case or partial check than an unrestricted bound. Whether the 2026 event is generated or assisted is a close call. The prior record (0.824 vs 0.842) is unresolved, but either way 0.8559 exceeds it.
